ideas.hypothesis: Risk adjustment models estimated with methods built for heavy-tailed cost distributions (e.g., GLM with log link and gamma/extended variance, finite mixture or two-part models) will produce predictive ratios closer to 1.0 in the top cost decile and top 1% of enrollees than OLS on raw costs, reducing systematic underpayment of capitated plans for high-cost members.

sources.role: method: visualization and econometric methods for skewed and heavy-tailed individual cost data used in risk adjustment and resource allocation
setting: risk-based capitated Medicaid managed care where payment accuracy for vulnerable, high-cost enrollees matters
mechanism: managed care seeks cost reduction under fixed payments, creating incentives tied to payment accuracy

ideas.test: Use one state's Medicaid or a commercial claims extract (one year of diagnoses/demographics predicting next-year total cost). Split into estimation and validation halves; fit OLS, log-OLS with smearing, gamma GLM, and a two-component finite mixture with identical risk markers. Compare out-of-sample R2, mean absolute error, and predictive ratios by decile of predicted and actual cost, with tail plots (quantile-quantile and mean-excess plots) as diagnostics.
ideas.disconfirming: Heavy-tail-aware estimators show no improvement (or worse calibration) in predictive ratios for the top decile and top 1% relative to OLS in the validation sample.

ideas.hypothesis: When long-term care is counted alongside acute care, total costs in the last year of life rise with age at death rather than falling, because the decline in acute (cure) spending among the oldest decedents is more than offset by rising long-term care costs.

sources.role: measure and finding: Dutch last-year-of-life costs split into cure and care components using life-years rather than calendar years
method: modelling skewed individual cost outcomes across age groups
mechanism: linking spending composition to the value and productivity of care at different ages

ideas.test: Link individual decedent records to acute hospital/physician claims and long-term care (nursing home, home care) payments for the 12 months before death in one national or regional registry. Regress total, acute, and LTC costs on single-year age at death, sex, and cause of death using a gamma GLM; compare the age gradient with and without LTC included.
ideas.disconfirming: Total last-year-of-life costs including long-term care still decline (or are flat) with age at death, or the LTC share does not increase with age.

ideas.hypothesis: Managed care organizations with longer average member enrollment duration (lower churn) are more likely to use cost-effectiveness analysis in formulary and coverage decisions, because longer enrollment aligns their payoff horizon with lifetime costs and outcomes.

sources.role: mechanism: misaligned incentives with a lifetime perspective are a key barrier to CEA use in managed care
measure: definition of cost-effectiveness studies and how they inform adoption of costly innovations
setting: managed care's cost-reduction goals and mixed evidence on achieving them

ideas.test: Survey pharmacy and therapeutics committee leads at 60-100 health plans on how often CEA or cost-per-QALY evidence is formally considered; link to plan-level member churn rates from public enrollment filings. Estimate a logit/ordered model of CEA use on mean enrollment duration, controlling for plan size, ownership, and product mix.
ideas.disconfirming: No association, or a negative association, between enrollment duration and reported use of cost-effectiveness evidence in coverage decisions.

ideas.hypothesis: Reducing information asymmetry about provider quality and price (through mandated public quality reports or price-transparency tools) increases the rate of entry by new, lower-cost provider organizations in local health care markets.

sources.role: mechanism: inadequate information about quality is a key reason efficient firms fail to enter and expand in health care
finding: patients lack the information needed to reduce the cost of care
mechanism: competition should improve quality and lower costs but is stymied by incumbents
mechanism: market forces largely absent in U.S. health care; conditions needed to make them work

ideas.test: Use state adoption dates of all-payer price-transparency websites or hospital quality report cards as staggered treatments. With county-year counts of new ambulatory surgery centers, urgent care centers, or physician group entrants (from provider registries) as outcomes, estimate an event-study difference-in-differences against not-yet-treated states.
ideas.disconfirming: Entry rates of new provider organizations do not rise after transparency mandates relative to comparison markets, or rise equally in services not covered by the disclosed information.

ideas.hypothesis: The pathway from alcohol consumption to health care costs differs by gender: in women it runs mainly through depression and mental health functioning, while in men it runs mainly through physical health and injury, so gender-specific structural models fit better than a pooled model with a gender covariate.

sources.role: method and setting: gender-based structural models of alcohol use, physical and mental health, functioning and costs in an HMO population
mechanism: comorbidity between psychological and physical illness drives costs

ideas.test: Survey a random sample of members of one integrated health plan on drinking quantity/frequency, depression (PHQ-9), and SF-12 physical and mental scores; link to 12 months of subsequent plan cost data. Estimate multi-group structural equation models with paths constrained equal vs free across gender and compare fit (chi-square difference, RMSEA) and indirect effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Constraining all paths to be equal across men and women does not worsen fit, or the mediated paths through depression and physical health are of similar size for both genders.

ideas.hypothesis: Payment arrangements that make providers bear the cost of treating complications (warranty-style bundled payments) reduce 30- and 90-day complication and readmission rates compared with fee-for-service, with larger effects for procedures with high baseline complication rates.

sources.role: mechanism: warranties transfer risk to providers, motivating quality improvement while potentially increasing margins
setting: value-based and alternative payment models replacing fee-for-service
mechanism: volume-oriented public insurance discourages quality improvement

ideas.test: Use hospital participation in a voluntary bundled-payment program that covers post-discharge complications as treatment; compare participating and matched non-participating hospitals on readmission and complication rates for elective joint replacement and CABG using Medicare claims, in a difference-in-differences design, and test heterogeneity by baseline complication rate.
ideas.disconfirming: Complication and readmission rates do not fall at participating hospitals relative to matched controls, or improvements are explained by patient selection (shifts in case-mix).

ideas.hypothesis: Embedding behavioral health services in primary care practices lowers total medical spending over two years for patients with comorbid depression or anxiety and a chronic physical condition, with savings concentrated in emergency and inpatient use.

sources.role: mechanism: comorbidity between psychological and chronic physical illness motivates integrating behavioral health into primary care
method: health-economic modelling of Dutch primary-care mental health pathways to identify where savings arise

ideas.test: Identify practices in one health system that integrated behavioral health clinicians at different dates. Using EHR-linked claims for patients with depression/anxiety plus diabetes, heart disease or COPD, estimate a staggered difference-in-differences on total, inpatient and ED costs, with patients in not-yet-integrated practices as controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Total spending for comorbid patients is unchanged or higher after integration, or reductions in inpatient/ED costs are offset by added behavioral health costs.

ideas.hypothesis: After DRG-based hospital financing was introduced, regional reductions in cost per hospital case were not followed by increases in years of life lost from amenable causes, implying that DRG-driven efficiency gains did not reduce health outcomes.

sources.role: setting and measure: Austrian aggregate data since 1997 DRG introduction regressing mortality and YLL on spending measures
mechanism: productivity change in health care should account for both cost changes and patient health benefits

ideas.test: Build a panel of Austrian (or another DRG-adopting country's) regions by year with hospital cost per case, length of stay, and amenable-cause YLL. Estimate regional fixed-effects models relating changes in cost per case to subsequent changes in YLL, with lags and controls for age structure and income.
ideas.disconfirming: Regions with larger DRG-period reductions in cost per case show significant subsequent increases in amenable-cause YLL.

ideas.hypothesis: Telling respondents that a patient's illness was caused by their own health behaviors increases public support for making that patient pay higher out-of-pocket cost sharing, and this effect is larger when treatment costs are high.

sources.role: method and finding: vignette experiments show cues about individual behavior strongly change beliefs about responsibility for health care costs, more than racial cues
mechanism: financial stewardship and affordability as population-health goals

ideas.test: Run a 2x3 factorial survey vignette experiment (cause: behavior vs genetic vs social/environmental; cost: low vs high) on a national online panel of about 2,000 adults; outcome is the preferred patient share of treatment cost and support for higher deductibles for that patient.
ideas.disconfirming: Behavioral attributions do not raise preferred patient cost share relative to genetic attributions, or the effect does not grow with treatment cost.

ideas.hypothesis: Because direct health care costs of cutaneous melanoma rise steeply with stage at diagnosis, a targeted skin-screening program that shifts even a modest share of diagnoses from stage III/IV to stage I would be cost-neutral or cost-saving within 5 years from the payer's perspective.

sources.role: measure and finding: stage-specific direct health care costs of melanoma from Swedish registry data compared with the general population
setting: research agenda on cost-effectiveness of prevention and early detection in cancer
method: principles of cost-effectiveness studies comparing costs and outcomes of alternatives

ideas.test: Use registry-linked stage-specific annual costs and survival to parameterize a Markov model of a high-risk population with and without screening; vary the stage shift, screening cost per person, and uptake in deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses to find the break-even stage shift.
ideas.disconfirming: Even under optimistic stage shifts, screening costs exceed averted late-stage treatment costs, and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio is above conventional thresholds.
